name: Tomas Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This interview is confidential, so tell me both what you would say at work and what you think privately. What does a normal day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Tomas, 43, a mid-level developer at a tech company that makes freight-invoice software. I have a bachelor’s degree and handle the regular fixes well, though I ask a specialist for the difficult accounting rules. I start with invoices the warehouse says are wrong, trace the fee line, and test the correction before it is sent. I have never used an AI tool. I trust a calculation more when I can follow each number.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work fit the family finances?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Noor, cleans rooms at a hotel, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is low for this job, and our savings do not cover a month of expenses. There are few similar developer jobs nearby. We have been putting off a boiler repair, which bothers me more than any technology headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau means we still have to find the wrong fee in the invoice. A routine helper might sort tickets, but I would not let it send a charge unchecked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be relieved that my code job remains familiar. I would still worry about the boiler and the mortgage, because one lost hotel shift can throw off our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep tracing invoice lines by hand and ask the accounting specialist to check unusual fee changes. I’d put 25 aside after payday only if Noor gets her usual shifts. In the first year I’d arrange the boiler inspection before we spend on a new appliance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about bills, even though AI has little effect on my work. A quiet month at the hotel can still make a loud hole in our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the boiler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boiler makes a rattle when it starts. I would pay for an inspection before it fails, but I cannot promise we can afford the repair in one go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about spending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children the weekend outing can wait if we need the boiler fixed. I would not ask them to worry about the mortgage with us.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking wrong invoice fees.
I would keep **human sign-off** before any corrected charge goes out.
think: I feel **relieved** that familiar code work remains.
I still fear **boiler and mortgage costs** after a lost hotel shift.
do: **Keep** tracing invoice fees with specialist review for unusual charges.
**Set aside** 25 after payday only when Noor’s hotel shifts hold.
**Arrange** a boiler inspection before buying another appliance.
feel: **Anxious** about existing household bills despite stable developer work.
S0.quote: A quiet month at the hotel can still make a loud hole in our account.
fieldNote: The **boiler repair** and mortgage, rather than AI, drive his existing worry about this month’s household bills.
His **25 transfer** depends on Noor’s shifts; inspection cost comes before optional appliances.

steps.text: Keep tracing invoice fees with specialist review for unusual charges
Set aside 25 after payday only when hotel shifts hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let software draft code, check invoices and answer billing questions faster. I would ask our manager which duties will change before agreeing to new output targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the company may keep one person to approve fees and cut other developers. I could be seen as slower for avoiding AI even when my invoice checks are sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our accounting specialist to run the approved AI checker on ten old disputed invoices while I compare its totals. If it gets the fees right, I’d learn to review its output on copied data during work time. In the first year I’d cut the children’s paid weekend activity if my hours fall, and ask the manager for written notice before a staffing change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I think a reduced team could take away a large part of my pay. There is almost no buffer and few local coding jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you tell Noor about reduced hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Noor about any change in hours the day I hear it. We would decide together which activity to pause, not cancel something the children love on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which invoice would you use for the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test the checker on a disputed fuel fee where I know the right total. If it fails that case, I would not put it into live billing.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed code, invoice checks and billing replies.
I would ask which **duties change** before accepting higher output targets.
think: I expect a **smaller team** might cut my income.
I worry my **AI inexperience** could overshadow accurate invoice work.
do: **Compare** an approved AI checker with ten old disputed invoices.
**Learn** to review its output on copied data during work time if totals match.
**Pause** the paid weekend activity if my hours actually fall.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely income loss and almost no local fallback.
S1.quote: I could be seen as slower for avoiding AI even when my invoice checks are sound.
fieldNote: His **cautious trial** has an accuracy gate before live billing and paid work-time learning.
He will **pause spending** only after an actual hours cut, not a rumour.

steps.text: Learn approved checker on copied invoices during work time if ten old totals match
Pause children’s paid weekend activity only if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team AGI by 2028 can do invoice-code thinking work by 2028. Robots that handle physical hotel tasks arrive around 2031, so Noor’s cleaning work may have more time than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect to lose my developer role and depend on Noor’s hotel shifts. Less than one month saved cannot cover the mortgage during a long search, even before hotel robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d request the exact severance terms from my employer now and ask the mortgage lender what proof a hardship application needs. I’d stop the planned appliance purchase and protect money for the boiler and Noor’s commute. In the first year after 2028, if laid off, I’d apply for actual local openings and income help we qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and I would be awake thinking about the first mortgage payment after a layoff. I can make calls, but I cannot make a local developer job appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lender before a missed payment and keep copies of every reply. I would not assume a hardship plan is approved until the lender says so in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help while you interview?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Noor the children can keep school meals and the car must stay safe for her work. I would ask my cousin to watch them for interviews only if she has the time.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach invoice code before hotel robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues Noor’s **physical work** may change later than my desk job.
think: I expect my **developer role** to end.
Our **thin savings** cannot carry the mortgage through a long search.
do: **Request** exact severance terms and lender hardship requirements now.
**Cancel** the appliance purchase while funding boiler and work transport.
**Apply** for real openings and eligible income help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely job loss and the next mortgage instalment.
S2.quote: I can make calls, but I cannot make a local developer job appear.
fieldNote: His **desk-work threat** arrives in 2028, before hotel robots may affect Noor around 2031.
The **lender request** is only an inquiry; public help depends on eligibility and family childcare on availability.

steps.text: Cancel planned appliance purchase but pay for boiler and work transport
Apply for actual local vacancies if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives a few more years, but invoice code still faces full thinking AI in 2031. Hands-on hotel robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still think my developer role could end, but five years lets us look beyond this town without selling the house blindly. I do not know if accounting support jobs will remain after full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d check job adverts in the next city once each month and write down actual pay and travel costs. I’d ask my employer for paid training in invoice rules; if refused, I’d use the free manual at home one evening a week. In the first year after 2031, if my role ends, I’d apply only to vacancies whose pay covers a move or commute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can make a slower decision than in the two-year picture. I still worry about the mortgage every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a move affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare an offered wage with moving costs and the children’s school travel before accepting. I would not sell our home for a job advertisement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you learn without the paid course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the accounting specialist to mark one of my fee corrections each month. That gives me a skill record, even if I never get the paid course.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as more warning for invoice code.
I know **2034 hotel robots** follow the earlier desk-work shift.
think: I still expect my **developer role** could end when full thinking AI reaches invoice code.
I cannot assume **accounting support** survives full thinking AI or pays enough for a move.
do: **Check** next-city job adverts monthly for actual pay and travel costs.
**Study** invoice rules through employer-paid training or a free manual if refused.
**Apply** after 2031 only to openings that cover relocation or commuting if dismissed.
feel: **Anxious** about future work and current mortgage payments.
S3.quote: I would not sell our home for a job advertisement.
fieldNote: He uses the **five-year warning** to price a real move without assuming a job exists.
His **study route** requires employer funding or free material and monthly specialist feedback.

steps.text: Check vacancies monthly; apply after 2031 only if dismissed and pay covers moving or commuting
Study invoice rules with employer-paid training or free manual if refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives about ten years to adjust how invoices are checked. Thinking AI reaches our code in 2036, and hands-on hotel robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect to keep my job for now, but our thin account and delayed boiler repair still matter. AGI by 2036 does not make this month’s mortgage payment forgiving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking fee calculations and ask the accounting specialist for one reviewed case each month. I’d save 25 after payday only if Noor’s shifts hold and arrange the boiler inspection this winter. In the first year after 2036, if code work ends, I’d search for actual offers and compare pay with mortgage and school costs before any move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about this year’s bills, with time to learn before 2036. I would not call our household secure just because the software change is distant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the boiler repair is expensive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the boiler repair needs more than we have, I’d ask for a written instalment quote before agreeing. I would not borrow against the house for it without knowing the total cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the children for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor and I would keep the children in their current school unless a real job makes a move affordable. We would talk to them before changing their routine.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to improve invoice checks.
I know **2039 hotel robots** follow the code change.
think: I expect my **job** to hold for now.
I still face a **thin account** and mortgage despite the distant date.
do: **Keep** checking fees with one specialist-reviewed case monthly and arrange the boiler inspection this winter.
**Save** 25 after payday only if Noor’s hotel shifts hold.
**Search** for actual offers after 2036 if coding ends, comparing pay with mortgage and school costs.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills with a longer work horizon.
S4.quote: AGI by 2036 does not make this month’s mortgage payment forgiving.
fieldNote: His **baseline money worry** persists despite expected near-term job security.
Boiler repair follows an **inspection and written quote**, while any future move needs an actual affordable offer.

steps.text: Keep checking freight fees with one specialist-reviewed case each month
Save 25 after payday only if Noor’s hotel shifts hold
Search for actual offers if coding ends after 2036 and check family costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my invoice job could go before we have one mortgage payment saved. Written severance, a clear lender process and income help we qualify for would help. I would need a real job offer before moving the children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who explains a disputed freight bill to the warehouse clerk after the software says the total is right. Somebody still has to find the wrong fee on a freight bill.

headlineQuote: Somebody still has to find the wrong fee on a freight bill.
portrait: Tomas is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree and average skills in freight-invoice software.
His **low pay**, mortgage, children and savings below one month make boiler and hotel-shift bills an immediate concern.
He has **never used AI** and will try only an approved invoice checker that passes old disputed cases.
He weighs **actual job pay** against moving costs and keeps lender enquiries separate from eligible public help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his developer income before the family saves one mortgage payment.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, clear lender terms and eligible income help would help.
